analysis.one_liner: Requires police to get a warrant before using facial recognition and bans its use in surveillance and immigration enforcement.
analysis.headline: The Facial Recognition Act of 2023 was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, was never taken up by either one, and died without a single vote when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 [S1][S4].
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put court oversight around police use of facial recognition: officers would generally need a warrant to search databases of driver's license, passport, and arrest photos against a face image. It would ban scanning body camera and drone footage, ban real-time face surveillance, ban using facial recognition to track people exercising First Amendment rights or to enforce immigration law, and require annual testing to prove the systems are accurate across race, gender, and age. It also gives people wrongly identified the right to sue for up to $50,000 per violation and lets courts throw out evidence obtained illegally. It never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote [S1][S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone whose photo sits in a government database — which is essentially every licensed driver — plus people wrongly identified by facial recognition. The bill's sponsor pointed to the risk that error-prone systems misidentify people, with documented disparities by race and gender, leading to wrongful stops and arrests. The notice provisions would tell people arrested via a facial recognition match which system and database flagged them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, crime suspects, and misidentified people

how_it_helps.text: Police could search reference photo databases (driver's license, passport, and arrest photos) only under a court order based on probable cause of a serious crime, after other investigative steps failed, with narrow emergency exceptions requiring prosecutor approval within 12 hours [S2].

The bill bans use of facial recognition on body camera, dashcam, and drone footage, bans real-time face surveillance, bans using it to track people exercising First Amendment rights, and bans its use for immigration enforcement [S2].

No agency could use a system that fails an annual National Institute of Standards and Technology accuracy and bias test, and any system whose accuracy varies significantly by race, ethnicity, gender, or age could be barred outright [S2].
Arrest photo databases would have to be purged every six months of photos of minors, people released without charge, people whose charges were dropped or dismissed, and people acquitted [S2].

People identified in violation of the bill could sue for the greater of the violator's profits or $50,000 per violation, plus attorney's fees; a private right of action would also cover discriminatory impact, and evidence from unlawful scans would be inadmissible in court [S2].

State and federal agencies would have to log and publicly report facial recognition searches — including arrests and convictions broken down by race, ethnicity, gender, and age — and submit to annual audits, with suspension of use if violations are found; states that refuse could lose 15 percent of their Bureau of Justice Assistance grant funds [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies would bear compliance costs: warrant applications, logging, annual testing, audits, and reporting. Facial recognition vendors would lose sales and face liability-adjacent exposure if their systems fail accuracy and bias benchmarks or get agencies sued.
analysis.who_pays_short: Police agencies and facial recognition vendors

drawbacks.text: The warrant requirement could add delay to identification work, though the bill preserves immediate use for identifying deceased or incapacitated people, victims, AMBER Alert subjects, booked arrestees, and emergencies involving imminent death or serious injury [S2].
The only financial penalty on states is a 15 percent reduction in one grant program for noncompliance, so an agency determined to keep using the technology has a limited downside [S2].

The enforcement scheme depends heavily on self-reporting by judges, prosecutors, and agencies, and on state governments designating independent auditors; the good-faith reliance on a court order is a complete defense to civil suits, which could blunt the private enforcement mechanism [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to ordinary people are substantial: a court-order gate before police scan driver's license and arrest photos of millions, testing that targets documented racial accuracy gaps, and a real remedy for people wrongly arrested. The costs fall mainly on police agencies and vendors in the form of paperwork, testing, and a smaller market. The design is imperfect — the 15 percent grant penalty is a modest stick, and self-reported data can understate violations — but the bill explicitly preserves stricter state laws rather than overriding them [S2].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary and Science committees on the day it was introduced, neither committee ever scheduled a hearing or vote, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 [S1][S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the bill with five Democratic cosponsors on October 26, 2023 [S1][S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee [S4].
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2025 [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police agencies and facial recognition vendors are better off: they continue using the technology with no warrant requirement, no mandatory accuracy or bias testing, no purging of arrest photos, and no public reporting of how the systems are used.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies and facial recognition vendors

sides.party_line_note: All six supporters on the record were Democrats; no Republican ever cosponsored, spoke for, or voted on the bill, and no committee or floor vote ever happened, so the opposition never had to register formally [S1][S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill requires annual accuracy and bias testing, bans face surveillance and body-camera scanning, and exposes agencies using deficient systems to suits — shrinking the police market these firms sell into. Their revenue comes from police scanning the faces of ordinary people, so their interest runs against the public's privacy interest here.

Agencies would lose unrestricted access to driver's license and arrest photo databases, face audits and public reporting disaggregated by race, and could have evidence suppressed. Discretion over a powerful investigative tool is the concentrated interest at stake; the accountability provisions are what ordinary people gain.

The bill amends the Driver's Privacy Protection Act to bar bulk transfers of license photos to facial recognition systems and to allow access only under a court order. DMV photo databases would stop being an open feed for police face searches.
